lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 8 -- The Influence Meeting
lesson.grammar_point: gerund and infinitive after verbs of influence

listenings.text: People confuse consensus with buy-in, and the confusion is expensive. Silence in a meeting almost never means agreement. It usually means somebody has decided that the conversation is not worth having in public, which is a very different thing. My test for real buy-in is simple, and it has nothing to do with what happens in the room. Would this person defend the idea in a room you are not in? If the answer is no, you do not have buy-in. You have politeness. The other thing I would tell anyone in your position is to name the trade-off yourself. Every proposal costs somebody something. If you name that cost, it reads as judgement and people trust the rest of what you say. If they find it, it becomes a weakness in your case and you spend the meeting defending instead of deciding. People who only present get surprised twice. Once when the proposal is approved, and again six months later when nothing at all has happened.

When I moved into a group where everything happened in English, my presentations were fine and my influence collapsed. It took me a year to understand why. Influence does not live in presentations. It lives in the unscripted conversations, and those were exactly the ones I was avoiding. A presentation you can prepare. A corridor has no agenda, no slides and no second draft, so everything that makes a presentation feel safe is missing. What I started doing sounds ridiculous and it worked. I prepared the informal conversations the way I prepared the formal ones. Three sentences, written on paper, before I picked up the phone. What I want, what it costs them, and what I am asking for specifically. The calls came out slightly stiff for the first month, and here is the part that surprised me: nobody minded. The awkwardness was entirely mine. It went away, and the influence came back.

extra_audio.text: Before I put this on an agenda, where would you land on it? I know what this costs your market. Let me tell you what it buys it. If this comes up when I am not in the room, would you be willing to get behind it? Two markets are already behind it, and what I need from you is the decision itself.

reading.rtitle: Note to File -- Exposure Limits, Pre-Board
paras: Ahead of Thursday, the limits proposal was socialised with four people rather than going straight onto the agenda. The order was deliberate: the sceptic first, the decision-maker last.

Group Finance avoided committing to a number but agreed to look at the reserving page before the meeting. Their objection was timing, not principle, and it is the objection most likely to appear in the room.

Henrik was told, before he could raise it, that tighter limits in the south would ration his own capacity. He recommended waiting for the reserving page and then offered to speak in support if the item came up in the presenter's absence. That commitment is recorded here because it is worth more than agreement.

By Wednesday two markets had got behind the proposal. The pre-read went out on Tuesday evening so that nobody would arrive unprepared. The group is now committed to reviewing the limits every quarter. No approval was sought for the portion already inside the regional mandate.
reading.source: Note to file -- Commercial Directorate, not for circulation
